# A fixed M/2^n moment-centroid obstruction by an actual convex layer lift

This note disproves the selector rule

    Choose ANY integer base j with D_j >= M/2^n;
    take the centroid of B_(M/2^n)(j).

The selected point need not have halfspace mass gamma_d M/2^n.
This is an obstruction to that selector, not to OC or to choosing some
different base. In this example a maximum-D base lies in the other layer.

## 1. The exact planar input, independently recomputed

Let A be the convex hull in coordinates (z,x) of

    {0} times [0,4],  {1} times [2,16],  {2} times [7,11].

The endpoint midpoint interval [7/2,15/2] is contained in [2,16].
Consequently these are exactly the integer fibers of A; no additional
part of the convex hull enlarges the middle sampled fiber. Its integer
projection is {0,1,2}, all fibers are positive, and A has nonempty
planar interior. The mixed length is 22.

At j=1 the marginal closed-halfspace depth in base space is D_j=18:
either closed half-line through 1 retains the middle length14 and one
endpoint length4. An interval of base mass selected with zero moment
about j has equal masses on the two endpoint fibers.

For t=18, the interval of continuous barycenters is exactly

    B_18(1)=[19/3,1873/216].                         (1)

Here is a direct certificate. For the upper endpoint select above

    x=5/6+(7/2)z.

The selected masses are 19/6,35/3,19/6 and have total18 and base mean1.
The continuous first moments are respectively

    551/72, 2135/18, 2147/72,

whose sum is 1873/12. Thus the barycenter is 1873/216. For every other
feasible density f, the pointwise threshold inequality

    [x-5/6-(7/2)z](1_H-f)>=0

integrates to the corresponding first-moment comparison: equal total
masses and base moments cancel the affine threshold. This proves
upper optimality.

For the lower endpoint select the whole endpoint intervals and [2,12]
in the middle fiber. These are the portions below

    x=12+(7/2)(z-1).

Their masses are 4,10,4 and their moments are 8,70,36. The total moment
is114, giving 19/3. The reversed threshold exchange inequality proves
lower optimality. The feasible density set is compact and convex, so
these two extrema prove (1), not merely bounds on it.

The ordinary centroid of (1) is

    y=3241/432.

Set v=1513/432. The closed halfspace

    H_0={x>=y+v(z-1)}

contains (1,y). Its thresholds at z=0,1,2 are

    4, 3241/432, 2377/216.

The z=0 contribution is one point of zero length; the z=2 threshold
is strictly above11. Thus

    mu_A(H_0)=16-y=3671/432 <9,                    (2)

with exact deficit 217/432 from9. This recomputes the certificate in
`candidate b438400a798308fc`.

## 2. The lifted full-dimensional body with six exact sampled fibers

Use integer coordinates (z,r) in R^2 and continuous coordinate x in R.
Let A' be the image of A under (z,x)->(z,(25/11)x). Define

    C=conv( {(z,0,x):(z,x) in A}
            union {(z,1,x):(z,x) in A'} ).

This is a compact full-dimensional convex body in R^3. For example A
contains a planar open ball, and joining it to its positive dilation
in the parallel layer r=1 produces three affinely independent
directions and hence nonempty three-dimensional interior.

Its projection onto the integer coordinate space is exactly
[0,2] times [0,1]. At r=0, any convex combination representing a point
of C has total weight zero on the r=1 layer. Therefore its section at
r=0 is EXACTLY A. Similarly its section at r=1 is EXACTLY A'. These
extreme-layer identities prevent any unintended enlargement of the
sampled fibers. There are no other integer r levels.

Hence the six integer fibers are

    r=0: [0,4],       [2,16],          [7,11],
    r=1: [0,100/11],  [50/11,400/11], [175/11,25],

at z=0,1,2 respectively. Their row masses are22 and50. Thus

    n=2, d=1, q=1, M=72, t=M/2^n=18.              (3)

The measure here is the actual H^1 mixed measure on these six fibers.

## 3. Exact moment body at a Doignon-qualified base

Take j=(1,0). If sigma<=mu_C has mass18 and base mean j, then

    integral r d sigma=0.

All sampled r coordinates are0 or1 and the measure is nonnegative.
Therefore sigma gives zero mass to the entire r=1 layer. Its remaining
constraint is exactly the original base moment integral z d sigma=18.
Conversely every original feasible mass18 selection in A is feasible
for C at j. Consequently

    B_18^C((1,0))=B_18^A(1),

with the same centroid y=3241/432.

Moreover D_j=18 exactly. Any closed integer-space halfspace containing
(1,0), restricted to r=0, either contains all that row or is a closed
half-line in z containing1. Its row0 contribution is at least18, so
D_j>=18. Conversely the base halfspace

    z-1-2r>=0

contains j, retains row0 bases1 and2, and excludes every row1 base.
It has mass18. Thus

    D_j=18=M/4,                                    (4)

so j satisfies precisely the weighted-Doignon mass requirement.

## 4. An explicit finite oblique ambient cap violating the selector target

Define the closed ambient halfspace

    H={ (z,r,x): x>=3241/432+(1513/432)(z-1)+40r }.

Its boundary contains (1,0,y). On row0 it is exactly H_0. On row1
its smallest threshold over z=0,1,2 is44, whereas the largest continuous
coordinate anywhere in that row is400/11<44. The entire added row is
therefore excluded by this explicit finite tilt.

Consequently

    mu_C(H)=3671/432
           <9
           =(1/2)18
           =gamma_1 M/2^2.                         (5)

All constants, fibers, and cap boundaries are exact. This proves failure
of the fixed-mass moment-body-centroid rule at this eligible base. No
numerical optimization or approximation is used.

## 5. Why this does not refute a maximum-depth base choice

The new row has total mass50. Even the elementary weighted median
bound gives it a base of row depth at least25>18. More precisely its
middle base has within-row depth

    (25/11)18=450/11.

Every ambient base halfspace containing (1,1) contributes at least
this much from row1. A sufficiently positive r tilt can exclude row0
while realizing the row1 half-line minimum; for example

    z-1+2(r-1)>=0

retains only row1 bases1,2. Hence the full marginal depth at (1,1) is
exactly450/11, greater than18. The six actual base depths are their
within-row depths, because each row is an exposed projection layer.
Thus a maximum-D rule selects (1,1), not the bad base (1,0).

This is a mass-accounting obstruction to using this padding argument
against every eligible or maximum-depth base. It does not establish
that either strengthened base-selection rule succeeds in other bodies.

## 6. General extreme-layer preservation mechanism

The construction has a useful exact general form. Let a convex body
A in R^n times R^d have mixed mass M, with d>=1. For any s>0 put a copy
of A in a new integer layer r=0 and its continuous dilation by s in
layer r=1, retaining all original integer coordinates, and take the
convex hull. The new mixed mass is

    M_new=(1+s^d)M.

At every base (j,0), its mass-t moment body is unchanged, because
nonnegative r and zero r-moment force all selected mass into the old
layer. Its marginal closed-halfspace capacity D_(j,0) is also exactly
D_j: restriction to the old layer gives the lower bound, and a finite
tilt excluding the new bounded layer gives the matching upper bound.

Whenever 2^(n+1)t>M, choose

    s^d=2^(n+1)t/M-1.

Then the NEW prescribed fixed mass M_new/2^(n+1) is exactly the old t.
Every bad selected-mass example at that t survives as a fixed-mass
selector obstruction in one more integer dimension, provided its old
base satisfied D_j>=t. An old cap can likewise be extended with a
finite excluding coefficient on r.

This preservation concerns one exposed-layer base. The added mass
can create better bases elsewhere, as it explicitly does above.
